extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in journalism ethics, editors, and those who follow retractions and media corrections
extracted.subtask_description: A news article describing Harper's Magazine's first formal retraction (of a 1998 Stephen Glass piece), explaining the factual basis, timeline, editorial reasoning, and related precedents. It summarizes the author's admission, the magazine's response, and broader implications for editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabrication of quotes, people, or entire stories
rubrics_metrics.description: "made up quotes, people, and even entire stories."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article identifies fabrication of quotes, invented people, and wholly fabricated narratives as clear grounds for retraction. The piece also notes Glass fabricated notes and lied about interviews, which are presented as explicit examples of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of fabrication determines need for full retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Harper's calculated the fabrications affect "at least 5,647 of the 7,902 words" (more than 70 percent) and stated: "A deception of that scale requires more than a simple enumerating of errors and falsehoods; we must retract the entire article."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a substantial majority of an article is based on fabrications, partial corrections are insufficient and the outlet should retract the entire piece. The magnitude of the deception is used as a primary criterion for full retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to confirm falsity before retracting (verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: "We can't retract the story without being able to confirm that it was false," said John R. MacArthur, Harper's president and publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the outlet cannot confirm a story's falsity (e.g., unverifiable anonymous sources or callers), it may decline to retract until verification is possible. Verification difficulties can delay or prevent retraction absent stronger evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-requested retraction and detailed admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephen Glass requested the retraction in a letter specifying the sections he fabricated and stating "I fabricated... I lied to the staff of Harper's." He included a disclaimer about possible omissions relying on his memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A direct admission by the author, especially with an itemized list of fabrications, is treated as valid grounds for retraction even many years later; however, the publisher may note limitations (e.g., reliance on the author's memory) when assessing completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated supporting materials and interviews as egregious misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass wrote: "In addition to the content of the article, I fabricated notes in support of this story. I lied to the staff of Harper's. I fabricated in interviews about this story. I engaged in egregious misconduct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating fake supporting documentation (notes) or fabricating interviews/sources is characterized as serious (egregious) misconduct that supports a decision to retract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction notice placement and archival handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Harper's "affixed a note to the article" and said it "won't remove it from our online archive, but we've stamped the digital version with the word retracted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions can be implemented by appending a prominent note or 'retracted' stamp to the digital archival copy rather than removing content entirely; publishing the author's letter and the outlet's response alongside the notice is another transparency practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective actions and restitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece notes Glass "repaid the magazine $10,000 — his fee for the piece, plus estimated interest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetary repayment or restitution by the author may accompany retraction as a corrective action, though such remediation is distinct from and does not replace the decision to mark or retract the work based on falsity or misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial commitment to fact-checking and prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: "That we’ve had to do this only once speaks to the excellent work of generations of fact-checkers. We remain committed to getting the story straight month after month, year after year — and to making sure no one like Stephen Glass is ever allowed to fool us again."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust fact-checking and ongoing editorial vigilance are presented as essential preventive measures; outlets frame retractions as failures the fact-checking system aims to minimize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-media precedent: removing/flagging content when truthfulness is in question
rubrics_metrics.description: This American Life "pulled three segments that involved [Glass]" and noted an episode was removed "because of questions about its truthfulness," with the segment retained only in the transcript for reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different media (print, radio, podcasts) may remove or flag content, and may retain transcripts or notes for record-keeping. Questions of truthfulness across formats justify removal or flagging and publication of explanatory notes.
